summary: When a Carrier Grade NAT or application proxy sits in the path, a remote server cannot tell which host behind a shared IP address sent a packet. This document collects potential solutions for revealing a host identifier (HOST_ID) unique to each host. It analyzes them without recommending one.

plainLanguage.summary: When many subscribers share one public IP address, the server at the far end cannot tell which subscriber sent a packet. This RFC reviews nine ways to send an extra identifier along with the packets, and finds that each one has limits. It makes no recommendation.

questions: identifying hosts behind shared ip address
subtitle: Nine ways to tell a remote server which subscriber behind a shared IP address sent a packet.

tldr.problem: When several subscribers share one public IP address, a remote server cannot tell which of them sent a packet, so blocking one misbehaving host blocks all of them.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC analyses nine channels for carrying a HOST_ID, an extra identifier that the address-sharing function adds: the IP Identification field, an IP option, a TCP option, an application header such as Forwarded, the PROXY protocol, port sets, HIP, a companion ICMP message and an out-of-band IDENT query.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational RFC with no recommendation, because the working group judged it too early to pick one. Its table shows that every option fails somewhere: on non-TCP traffic, on encrypted traffic, near the MTU size, behind a firewall, or when the server does not cooperate.

facts.label: HOST_ID uniqueness
facts.value: Unique per host under a shared address, not global

today: RFC 6967 is an Informational RFC published in June 2013. It has not been obsoleted or updated. It remains a survey of candidate ways to reveal a host identifier behind a shared address, with no recommendation attached.

sections.title: Why Shared Addresses Cause Trouble
sections.content:
Several problems appear when one IP address is shared among several subscribers. The RFC lists them as reported in RFC 6269: implicit identification, spam, blacklisting a misbehaving host, and redirecting users with infected machines to a dedicated portal. The contexts are Carrier-Grade NAT, application proxies, and Address plus Port (RFC 6346).

The sharpest case is a server that uses the source IPv4 address as an identifier, so that it can treat some incoming connections differently. With NAT44 (RFC 3022) or NAT64 (RFC 6146) in the path, that address is shared, and when the server sees packets from the same source address it cannot tell which host sent them. The IPv4 address alone is not enough to identify a host.

Leaving this unaddressed has costs. Operators of IP connectivity services spend more on operations, including the cost of calls to a hotline. Content providers lose revenue when users cannot reach them. Customers are unhappy, because the quality of their experience suffers and one subscriber's actions affect another's access. As a mitigation, it is worth looking for ways to disclose information that lets a remote server tell the hosts apart.

The purpose of this document is to analyse a set of alternative channels for conveying a host identifier and to assess how far each one solves the problem. The RFC is explicit that it makes no recommendation, because the working group felt it was too premature to include one.
sections.plainLanguage: When many subscribers share one public IP address, the server at the far end cannot tell which subscriber sent a packet. This RFC reviews nine ways to send an extra identifier along with the packets, and finds that each one has limits.

sections.title: What a HOST_ID Must Do
sections.content:
The RFC calls the extra information a HOST_ID. A server that applies policies based on the source IP address applies them to every host sharing that address, so blacklisting the address of a spammer also restricts everyone else behind it. The HOST_ID is the extra information a server needs to tell the sending hosts apart.

Several properties follow. The HOST_ID must be unique to each host under the same shared IP address, where possible; where only the home gateway is visible to the operator side of the translation function, it need only be unique to that gateway. It does not have to be globally unique, because the combination of the public source address and the identifier is what ends up unique. Within this document a host is any computer behind a home gateway or directly connected to the address-sharing function, which in most cases is the home gateway itself.

Where the identifier travels depends on the layer. If it is carried at the IP level, every packet has to bear it. If it is carried at a connection-oriented layer above, the identifier is needed once during session establishment, for example in a TCP three-way handshake, and every packet in that session is then attributed to the HOST_ID chosen at the start.

The document assumes that the operator-side address-sharing function injects the HOST_ID. An alternative, to avoid possible performance loss, is for the host or home gateway to inject its own identifier and for the address-sharing function to check the value, much as an IP anti-spoofing function would. Some proposals instead retrieve the identifier through an out-of-band mechanism or signal it in a dedicated notification channel. A HOST_ID can be ambiguous for a host with several interfaces or several addresses on one interface, and identifiers that differ should not be read as proof that two end systems are different.
sections.plainLanguage: A HOST_ID only has to be unique among the hosts that share one address, not across the Internet. It can travel in every packet or just once when a connection is set up.

sections.title: HOST_ID and Privacy
sections.content:
Address sharing has been used for years to conserve public IPv4 addresses, with customer premises equipment that gives a whole household one public address and translates private addresses with NAT. With the exhaustion of IPv4 address space, sharing between customers on a much larger scale is likely to become more prevalent. Some users are unaware of whether their unique address is revealed, while others take privacy benefits from sharing, because it makes the actions of all users behind the NAT unattributable to any single host.

The proposals here help differentiate hosts that share an address, and how much they differentiate depends on what the HOST_ID contains. The identifier is as volatile as the internal IP address: the address-sharing function may use a new one when the host reboots or gets a new internal address. As with persistent IP addresses, persistent HOST_IDs make it easier to track a user over time.

The RFC does not want hosts to become more identifiable than they would be with a dedicated public address, but depending on the solution the HOST_ID may make a device easier to fingerprint. It therefore recommends limiting HOST_IDs to local rather than global uniqueness, and not using permanent HOST_ID values. If several solutions are combined and each carries different pieces of information, fingerprinting gets even easier, so a function that injects identifiers at several layers should reveal the same subset of information at each layer. For example, if one layer references the lower 16 bits of an IPv4 address, the other layer should reference those 16 bits too.

A HOST_ID can be spoofed, just as an IP address can, and users of anonymity services such as Tor may be able to strip HOST_ID information before it reaches its destination. To control what is revealed, the address-sharing function should be able to strip, rewrite and add HOST_ID fields, and it may be configured to disable injection for some users. A HOST_ID specification should explain the privacy impact of what it specifies: the extent of uniqueness and persistence, assumptions about the lifetime of the identifier, whether and how it can be obfuscated or recycled, whether location information can be exposed, and the effect on device fingerprinting.
sections.plainLanguage: Sharing an address hides who sent a packet, and some users rely on that. A HOST_ID must not undo it more than necessary, so it should be unique only within the shared address, and it should not be permanent.

sections.title: Nine Ways to Carry a HOST_ID
sections.content:
The RFC analyses nine alternatives, describes what each one would look like, and sets out where it breaks down.

  • The IP Identification field. The address-sharing function rewrites the 16-bit IP-ID so that it identifies the host, following the rules of RFC 6864. The RFC calls this ill-advised, because it conflicts with the field's use for fragment reassembly and with the updated handling rules, because it is hard when packets arrive fragmented, and because it would disturb coordination between several NATs.
  • A new IP option. An IP option could carry the identifier and would work for any transport protocol, but routers and middleboxes commonly drop or strip unknown IP options, and injection adds complexity when the packet is at or close to the MTU size or the options space is exhausted. The RFC concludes that it is not viable.
  • A new TCP option. The identifier goes into a TCP option in the SYN packet, so no application has to change, but only TCP applications benefit. The reported failure ratio was 0.103% among the top 100,000 websites. Putting the identifier in the SYN consumes more header space; putting it in an ACK consumes only two bytes in the SYN, but then the server must wait for the ACK before sending data, and it can raise MTU problems.
  • Application headers. For HTTP, the Forwarded header can carry the original IPv4 address or IPv6 prefix, and the address-sharing device must strip any Forwarded headers it receives before adding its own. Only a subset of protocols can use this, it adds complexity when the HTTP message is near the MTU size, and injecting it for all HTTPS traffic is infeasible.
  • The PROXY protocol. A line of text beginning with PROXY is inserted at the start of the application data stream whatever the protocol, and the server removes it on receipt. It needs no application-specific knowledge, but a server that does not support it fails the session, and firewalls get in the way. The RFC calls it infeasible.
  • Port sets. Each host is given a restricted port set under the shared address, advertised by offline means. No new fields are needed, but it can contradict port randomisation and it is less efficient for third-party services when the port set is not advertised.
  • The Host Identity Protocol. HIP introduces its own namespace for identity, but it needs both the client and the server to support it, and the alternative of making the address-sharing function a HIP relay assumes that all servers are HIP-enabled.
  • A notification channel. The identifier is carried in a separate ICMP Echo Request sent alongside the session setup, describing the five-tuples as seen on both sides of the address-sharing function. It works for any transport protocol that uses a port number, and blocking the ICMP does not break the user connection, but cascaded NAT produces several ICMP messages and the server has to decide which identifier to use.
  • An out-of-band query. The Identification protocol is used to ask the address-sharing function for the identifier when a connection arrives. It is specific to TCP, needs an IDENT server inside the address-sharing function, and the connection may be delayed while the query is answered.
sections.plainLanguage: The nine options put the identifier in the IP header, in a TCP option, in an application header, in a text prefix on the connection, in the port number, in a separate ICMP message, or in a separate query. Each one breaks in a different way.

sections.title: Synthesis: Comparing the Options
sections.content:
Table 1 of the RFC brings the alternatives together. For each one it records whether the solution works over UDP, TCP, HTTP and encrypted traffic, the ratio of successful communications with remote servers, the expected performance impact, whether the server's TCP/IP stack has to be modified, and whether the solution can be generalised without any constraint on current architectures and practices.

Some figures need their explanation. The success ratio is the ratio of successful communications with remote servers when the identifier is injected with that solution. The port set and HTTP header solutions reach 100%, because neither needs an additional Layer 3 or Layer 4 field to carry the identifier. The ICMP and IDENT ratios are implementation specific but likely close to 100%: a server that does not support the mechanism ignores the companion message, while an upgraded server waits for it before accepting a session. The PROXY and HIP ratios are low because neither is widely deployed. The IP-ID ratio is theoretical, and assumes the address-sharing function follows the rules for rewriting the IP Identification field.

The performance column estimates the expected degradation from the processing needed at the IP layer. The notes explain the rest. Some solutions need a mechanism to advertise that a NAT takes part in the scheme, for example a DNS PTR record. The HTTP header solution is already widely deployed, by HTTP servers and load balancers. The HIP solution needs HIP-compliant clients and servers and deployed HIP infrastructure. The IP-ID solution is marked as a theoretical construct that is not documented, while several of the others are documented proposals.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC's table compares the nine options on whether they work for UDP, TCP, HTTP and encrypted traffic, how often a connection still succeeds, how much they slow things down, and whether they can be deployed without changing today's architecture.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
If the server trusts the content of the HOST_ID field, a third-party user can be impacted by a misbehaving user revealing a faked HOST_ID, such as a made-up original IP address. The same security concern applies to the injection of an IP option, a TCP option and application-related content such as the Forwarded HTTP header.

The HOST_ID may also be used to leak information about the internal structure of a network behind an address-sharing function. If the network administrator does not want that behaviour, the address-sharing function can be configured to strip any existing HOST_ID in packets received from internal hosts. HOST_ID specification documents should go further and elaborate on the threats inherent in each individual solution used to convey the identifier, such as the use of the IP-ID field to count hosts behind a NAT.
sections.plainLanguage: A server that trusts the identifier can be fooled by a user who fakes one, and the identifier can reveal the shape of the network behind it. The operator can turn off the injection or strip incoming identifiers.
